                                      PROJECT NO. 58481

 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                           §   PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                        §
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA § 37.0561                    §                OF TEXAS
                                                   §


  ROWAN DIGITAL INFRASTRUCTURE LLC COMMENTS ON STAFF’S SECOND
              DRAFT DISCUSSION RULE IN 16 TAC § 25.194

       Rowan Digital Infrastructure LLC (“Rowan”), acting on its own behalf and on behalf of its
project-level subsidiaries that are developing data centers in ERCOT, welcomes the opportunity
to provide feedback in response to the Public Utility Commission of Texas (“Commission”) Staff’s
second discussion draft of the new 16 Texas Administrative Code (“TAC”) § 25.194 implementing
Senate Bill 6 (“SB 6”) and Public Utility Regulatory Act (“PURA”) § 37.0561 large load
interconnection (“LLI”) standards (the “Discussion Draft”).


                                        I.      INTRODUCTION
       Rowan supports Staff’s general approach in this Discussion Draft. Rowan appreciates
Staff’s time during the January 9th workshop on Project 58481 (“workshop”) and Staff’s work on
the second discussion draft rule for 16 TAC § 25.194. Rowan offers the below comments to
provide additional context and perspective from its experience as an entity that develops, owns,
and operates large data centers through long-term leases with tenants.


                            II.     RESPONSES TO STAFF QUESTIONS
 3. Should the commission maintain the definition for an interconnecting utility that is set
     forth in Attachment C? If not, what definition should be used
   Rowan recommends that the Commission revise the definition of “interconnecting utility” to
distinguish between the roles of the interconnecting transmission service provider (“TSP”) that
conducts the large load interconnection study (“LLIS”) and the role of the retail distribution service
provider (“DSP”) that has the obligation to provide retail electric delivery service to the large load
customer’s load, as those may be two separate entities with distinct roles.
   The current proposed definition focuses on service area certification by defining
“interconnecting utility” as the “electric utility, municipally owned utility, or electric cooperative
 that is certificated to serve the interconnecting large load customer at retail or, if the certificated
utility designates, the interconnecting transmission service provider.” This unnecessarily
complicates the LLI process. Designating the retail DSP as the “interconnecting utility” is not
consistent with how the interconnection process works, as the retail DSP does not own or operate
the transmission facilities to which the large load customer seeks to interconnect, and the retail
DSP is not responsible for conducting the required interconnection studies.
    Although it would be appropriate for the large load customer or interconnecting TSP to keep
the retail DSP informed of an interconnection request (if the interconnecting TSP is a separate
entity from the retail DSP), the interconnection-related communications and agreements should be
directly between the large load customer and the interconnecting TSP, which owns and operates
the facilities necessary to interconnect to the large load customer to the Electric Reliability Council
of Texas (“ERCOT”) transmission network.
    Additionally, all of Senate Bill (“SB”) 6’s references to the “interconnecting electric utility”
refer to the utility that physically interconnects the load to the transmission system, not the utility
certificated to serve the interconnecting large load customer at retail. Notably, SB 6 requires a
large load customer to disclose to the interconnecting electric utility information about the
customer’s on-site backup generating facilities, which the interconnecting electric utility must
provide to ERCOT.1 Providing such disclosure to ERCOT would typically be the responsibility of
the interconnecting TSP that works directly with ERCOT on the interconnection process. In
general, the duties and responsibilities that fall on the interconnecting electric utility in PURA §
37.0561 are in the context of facilitating transmission interconnection, and have nothing to do with
the retail service that will be provided once the interconnection is complete. Thus, in this rule, the
“interconnecting utility” should be the TSP that owns and operates the facilities necessary to
interconnect a large load customer to the ERCOT transmission network, not the utility certificated
to serve the large load customer at retail, if the interconnecting TSP and retail DSP are different
entities.
    Accordingly, Rowan recommends the following modifications to the definitions:
    (6) Interconnecting utility — The transmission service provider that owns and operates the
    facilities necessary to interconnect a large load customer to the ERCOT transmission network.
    An interconnecting utility is not a distribution service provider if it is not also the transmission

        1
            See Public Utility Regulatory Act (“PURA”) § 37.0561(e).


                                                   Page 2 of 8
     service provider for the applicable interconnecting large load customer. is certificated to serve
    the interconnecting large load customer at retail or, if the certificated utility designates, the
    interconnecting transmission service provider.

    (14) Distribution service provider — the electric utility, municipally owned utility, or electric
    cooperative that is certificated to provide retail electric delivery service to the large load
    customer’s consuming facilities.

    (15) Transmission service provider — has the meaning given in 16 Texas Administrative
    Code § 25.5(142).


  4. If the commission maintains the definition for an interconnecting utility that is set
      forth in Attachment C, what framework should the rule establish for ensuring that
      the interconnecting transmission service provider receives the required security and
      CIAC in instances where the certificated retail utility and interconnecting
      transmission service provider are different entities?
      As noted above, Rowan strongly encourages the Commission to consider and recognize the
distinct roles of the TSP and DSP. In cases where these entities differ, Rowan recommends that
the rule expressly allow for a three-party Large Load Interconnection Agreement (“LLIA”)
between the customer, TSP, and DSP, with the TSP acting as the “interconnecting utility” for
purposes of receiving financial security and CIAC payments related to interconnection, and with
the DSP retaining its retail service obligations. 2 This framework will help ensure clarity and
efficiency in the allocation and collection of required financial security and CIAC payments. It
will also make clear that the interconnecting TSP is responsible for the LLIS and construction of
the interconnection facilities.


  5. Currently, ERCOT Planning Guide §9.2.1(1)(b) requires a large load customer to
      follow the criteria subject to the large load interconnection study process if the large
      load customer modifies an existing load facility that increases the aggregate peak
      demand of the facility by 75 MW or more. Should the commission maintain this


        2
          Rowan supports the three-party agreement concept recommended by Crusoe Energy Systems LLC at the
January 9 workshop.


                                               Page 3 of 8
      threshold for purposes of the rule? Or should any modification that increases the
     aggregate peak demand of the facility to 75 MW or more be required to satisfy the
     criteria in the rule?
     Rowan recognizes the need to clarify the application of the LLI process to existing large
load customers that request load increases. However, Rowan urges the Commission to be
cautious of unnecessarily restricting the ability of proven and legitimate large load customers
with existing loads to sustainably expand or scale their services. Accordingly, Rowan supports
an approach that would only subject existing large load customers to the LLI process (1) if a
customer with an existing facility below 75 MW requests an expanded interconnection that
would increase total peak demand at the site to 75 MW or above or (2) a customer with an
existing facility above 75 MW submits a modification request that would add 75 MW or more of
load to a single site within a two-year period.


 7. Does an interconnecting utility, at the intermediate agreement phase, have sufficient
     information to be able to estimate the costs of significant equipment and services and
     to estimate contribution in aid of construction?

           a. If so, should the rule require payment of the $100,000 per megawatt security
               at the time the request for interconnection is submitted? And require
               estimated security for significant equipment and services and contribution in
               aid of construction at the intermediate agreement stage, subject to a true up
               based on actual costs identified at the interconnection agreement stage?
   Rowan supports the use of financial commitments to cull speculative projects from the
interconnection queue. However, Rowan believes that the $100,000 per megawatt (“MW”)
financial security requirement is too high and may unnecessarily restrict large load development.
Rowan notes that multiple stakeholders raised similar concerns at the workshop. For example, the
Data Center Coalition (“DCC”) and Black Mountain Energy Storage (“Black Mountain”) stated
that a $100,000 per MW financial security requirement was too high, and Black Mountain said
that such a requirement could unintentionally kill projects that are otherwise financially viable.
Similarly, CenterPoint agreed that a $100,000 per MW financial security requirement could be
excessive and noted that a customer might have to post financial security that far exceeds the actual




                                            Page 4 of 8
 cost of interconnection. (For example, CenterPoint noted that a 2.5 GW project currently in the
interconnection queue could pay millions of dollars in financial security.)
   Instead of adopting the $100,000 per MW requirement, Rowan urges the Commission to
impose a financial security requirement based on either (a) a cost-based framework designed to
match financial security requirements to estimated CIAC, (b) a tiered dollar per MW scale capped
at $20,000 per MW, or (c) a percentage of the estimated costs to design, procure, and construct the
TSP’s interconnection facilities (“TIF”) to interconnect the large load customer. In particular,
option (c) would ensure that the cost of financial security is tied to the TSP’s actual expected
interconnection costs. If a large load customer seeks to interconnect in an area where minimal
utility buildout is required, a per MW security could grossly exceed the utility’s cost exposure.
The required financial security should accurately reflect the utility’s actual cost exposure.
   Additionally, Rowan asks the Commission to expressly allow surety bonds, corporate
guarantees, and comparable financial instruments as acceptable forms of financial security, in
addition to cash, letters of credit, and parent company guarantees. This approach achieves a better
balance between reducing speculative load interconnection requests while ensuring that financial
security requirements are aligned with project costs, which facilitates more efficient project
financing.
   Additionally, Rowan recommends that a large load customer’s tenant should be able to post
the required financial security (in lieu of the customer posting such security), provided that there
is a written contract between the large load customer and the tenant that obligates the tenant to
provide the required financial security. That would reflect the current reality that sometimes the
tenant, not the large load customer itself, chooses to assume the obligation to pay the required
financial security.


   8. Should the commission expand the criteria for demonstrating site control to include
       either site control over an electrical substation combined with exclusive development
       rights at a designated interconnection point or an exclusivity agreement with an
       existing generation resource for a proposed net metering arrangement?
   Yes, the Commission should expand the list of allowable site control methods to include (1)
site control over an electrical substation combined with exclusive development rights at a
designated interconnection point or (2) an exclusivity agreement with an existing generation



                                            Page 5 of 8
 resource for a proposed net metering arrangement. This approach provides clarity and flexibility
for developers approaching varied and unique project sites. Regarding the first option, Rowan
further recommends that it should be allowable for a customer to document site control over an
electrical substation by providing a letter of intent as proof of exclusive development rights.


    10. How should an interconnecting utility treat interest accrued from cash security?
         a. What interest rate should apply?
        Rowan recommends that an interconnecting utility should be required to pay interest
upon the refund of cash security at a defined rate, such as the federal funds rate band or a tariff-
specified metric. This practice is common in other utility contexts and ensures that customers are
fairly compensated for the time value of money while their funds are held as security.


    12. For what period of time should a large load customer be expected to operate after
        energization but before the interconnecting utility issues a final refund of any unused
        security, collateral, or CIAC in order to balance the state’s interests in supporting
        business development and minimizing the potential for stranded infrastructure costs?
    Rowan urges the Commission to clarify refund triggers so that a large load customer is not
required to reach its full contracted peak demand to receive a financial security or CIAC refund.
Instead, refunds should be tied to milestone-based risk reduction, such as the payment of CIAC
or the achievement of project milestones such as energization. This would better reflect actual
risk reduction and allow customers to recover funds in a timely and equitable manner.
Additionally, a customer’s financial security and CIAC should be refunded if the customer
withdraws the interconnection request, minus any costs incurred by the interconnecting utility to
study or construct facilities for the large load project.


    13. If the commission adopts a process whereby ERCOT, not the interconnecting utility,
        reallocates capacity on a system-wide basis through a batch study process, what
        parameters should the commission establish for such a process?
    Rowan does not take a specific stance on the potential ERCOT process to reallocate capacity.
However, Rowan does caution the Commission that an interconnecting utility should have the
flexibility to work with large load customers on their process for progressing to their requested



                                              Page 6 of 8
 capacity, as Oncor noted in the January 9 workshop. In Rowan’s experience, such flexibility has
been crucial in resolving capacity allocation issues and ensuring that facility needs are met
efficiently. Additionally, a large load customer tends to narrow in on its precise power
requirements closer to energization, so the parties—including the utility—need flexibility
regarding reallocation. This flexibility helps ensure that the parties have sufficient time to ramp
in, and to adjust based on the technology that is available and used at the time of energization.
Any reallocation process should preserve this utility-customer flexibility and avoid imposing
rigid, one-size-fits-all parameters.
   14. Is 60 days a sufficient time frame for an interconnecting utility to issue a required
       refund?
   Rowan supports a 60-day timeline for an interconnecting utility to issue a required refund to a
large load customer. However, Rowan notes that the 60-day time frame should begin when the
refund amount is determined, which may be after a true-up has been conducted. This approach
provides a reasonable balance between the interconnecting utility’s administrative needs and the
customer’s expectation for timely return of funds.




Dated January 16, 2026




                                              Respectfully submitted,




                                              ROWAN DIGITAL INFRASTRUCTURE LLC




                                            Page 7 of 8
                                    EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
   Discussion Question 3: Rowan recommends that the Commission define “interconnecting utility”
    as the TSP that owns and operates the facilities necessary to interconnect a large load customer to
    the ERCOT transmission network, rather than the retail DSP, to reflect the actual roles in the
    interconnection process.
   Discussion Question 4: If the TSP and DSP are different, Rowan supports a three-party agreement
    where the TSP receives security and CIAC payments and is responsible for the interconnection,
    while the DSP retains its retail obligations, ensuring clarity and efficiency.
   Discussion Question 5: Rowan supports only subjecting existing large load customers to the LLI
    process if a modification increases the site’s total peak demand to 75 MW or more, or if a single
    site’s load increases by 75 MW or more within two years, to avoid unnecessarily restricting
    legitimate customer expansions.
   Discussion Question 7: Rowan believes the proposed $100,000/MW financial security is excessive
    and recommends a cost-based, tiered, or percentage-based approach tied to actual interconnection
    costs, and supports allowing surety bonds and corporate guarantees as acceptable financial security.
    Additionally, a tenant should be allowed to post the required security.
   Discussion Question 8: Rowan supports expanding allowable site control methods to include
    control over a substation with exclusive development rights or an exclusivity agreement with an
    existing generation resource for net metering, which would provide developers with needed
    flexibility.
   Discussion Question 10: Rowan recommends that interconnecting utilities pay interest on
    refunded cash security at a defined rate, such as the federal funds rate, to fairly compensate
    customers for the time value of money.
   Discussion Question 12: Refunds of financial security or CIAC should be based on milestone
    achievements, such as energization or CIAC payment, rather than requiring full contracted demand,
    and should also be available if a customer withdraws, less any incurred costs.
   Discussion Question 13: Rowan urges that any ERCOT-led capacity reallocation process should
    preserve the flexibility for utilities and customers to work together on capacity allocation, rather
    than imposing rigid, universal rules.
   Discussion Question 14: Rowan supports a 60-day deadline for issuing refunds, starting from the
    determination of the refund amount (post-true-up), to balance administrative needs and customer
    expectations for timely fund return

Additionally, a tenant should be allowed to post the required security.
Discussion Question 8: Rowan supports expanding allowable site control methods to include
control over a substation with exclusive development rights or an exclusivity agreement with an
existing generation resource for net metering, which would provide developers with needed
flexibility.
Discussion Question 10: Rowan recommends that interconnecting utilities pay interest on
refunded cash security at a defined rate, such as the federal funds rate, to fairly compensate
customers for the time value of money.
Discussion Question 12: Refunds of financial security or CMC should be based on milestone
achievements, such as energization or CIAC payment, rather than requiring full contracted demand,
and should also be available if a customer withdraws, less any incurred costs.
Discussion Question 13: Rowan urges that any ERCOT-led capacity reallocation process should
preserve the flexibility for utilities and customers to work together on capacity allocation, rather
than imposing rigid, universal rules.
Discussion Question 14: Rowan supports a 60-day deadline for issuing refunds, starting from the
determination of the refund amount (post-true-up), to balance administrative needs and customer
expectations for timely fund return
